content.text: {"relation":"REFINED","consensus_summary":"Across all four blind responses the primary meaning is: deeds performed in obedience to the Mosaic law (Torah), especially when relied upon as the basis or means of justification before God; Paul denies these can justify, contrasting them with faith in Christ. Live disputes concern scope: works-righteousness generally (Reformation reading), Jewish boundary markers (New Perspective), ceremonial precepts only (Catholic/Thomistic), or halakhic rulings (4QMMT parallel).","book_summary":"The book defines 'works of the law' generically as deeds performed under an obligation imposed by any law or decree, with context determining whose law and which duty; it stresses that fulfilling such an obligation, while it may be obedience, places the lawgiver under no debt and earns no benefit. The book acknowledges the common teaching (deeds required by the Mosaic law set against faith) as the view it is qualifying.","consensus_core_identification":"Deeds done in obedience to the Mosaic law, treated as a (failed) basis for justification before God, contrasted with faith.","book_core_identification":"Deeds performed under a legally imposed obligation (whatever law or decree the context specifies), which as obligated duty cannot indebt the lawgiver or earn any benefit.","core_relation":"BOOK_BROADENS","extension_relation":"BOOK_SUPERSET","boundary_disagreement":"The consensus fixes the referent to the Mosaic Torah (with debate only over which parts or aspects). The book removes the Mosaic restriction from the definition itself, admitting deeds obligated by any law or decree and making the Mosaic identification a context-dependent instance rather than the meaning. It also shifts the emphasized failure mode: not merely 'cannot justify' but the more general principle that obligated performance creates no debt or merit owed by the lawgiver — a mechanism claim the consensus states only implicitly under the works-righteousness reading.","material_contradiction":"None. The book does not deny that in Paul's contexts the law in view is the Mosaic law; it subsumes that case under a broader category. Its no-debt/no-merit principle is compatible with, and arguably a generalization of, the consensus's anti-justification-by-works claim.","rationale":"Both readings identify the same central category — deeds performed in fulfillment of legal obligation that cannot earn standing with the lawgiver — so the referent is preserved, not replaced. But the book materially changes the extension by unmooring the phrase from the Mosaic Torah specifically ('whose law' is contextual), admitting cases the mainstream definition excludes. This resembles Response C's and D's listed alternative ('any human works/efforts, not limited to Mosaic Law'), which is recognized but non-primary, confirming this is a boundary shift within a recognized field rather than a novel or contradictory identification. Hence REFINED with a broadened core and superset extension.","citation_support":"PARTIAL","strongest_objection":"All seven printed citations (Rom 3:20, 28; 9:32; Gal 2:16; 3:2, 5, 10) occur in contexts where 'the law' is unambiguously the Mosaic Torah; none demonstrates the book's generalized 'any law or decree' definition, and the no-debt principle would be better supported by Romans 4:4, which is not cited. One could therefore argue the book's distinctive move outruns its own proof-texts — or, conversely, that since every cited instance concerns the Mosaic law, the book's definition collapses in practice to the consensus reading and should be classed as MATCH.","confidence":"medium"}
